story.headline: Xi meets Trump at the White House
story.summary: Xi Jinping began his first US state visit in a decade with a White House summit and state dinner as the two extended their trade truce.
story.display_body: Chinese President Xi Jinping opened his first US state visit in a decade on Thursday 24 September with a White House summit and state dinner with Donald Trump, as the two governments announced a two-month extension of their trade truce. Xi landed in Washington on Wednesday for a visit running through 25 September and was met with an unusual planeside welcome from Trump; the leaders' main meeting and a state dinner fall on Thursday. Ahead of the talks, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the two sides had agreed to extend the "Busan Agreement" — the economic détente between the countries that was due to expire on 10 November — by two months, easing the immediate threat of renewed tariff escalation. The agenda runs beyond trade to advanced technology and export controls, rare-earth minerals, Taiwan, Iran and the war in Ukraine; Beijing has pressed Washington to say it "opposes" rather than merely "does not support" Taiwanese independence, a one-word shift the US has resisted.
story.why: It is the highest-profile US–China encounter in years, and a durable tariff truce would steady a trade relationship whose swings ripple through Europe — including Switzerland — but the substantive disputes over chips, Taiwan and rare earths remain unresolved and the warmth of the optics should not be read as agreement on them.

story.headline: Judge orders White House to restore press access
story.summary: A federal judge granted a temporary order requiring the Trump administration to restore White House access for CNN, MS NOW and Politico.
story.display_body: A US federal judge on Thursday 24 September ordered the Trump administration to immediately restore White House access for CNN, MS NOW and Politico, granting a temporary restraining order against the ban the three outlets are suing over. District Judge Timothy Kelly — himself a Trump nominee from the president's first term — found the news organisations likely to succeed on the merits, including a due-process violation, and rejected the administration's national-security justification as lacking "factual support," stressing the public interest in a free press. The order runs for 14 days pending further proceedings. It follows Trump's 18 September move to revoke the outlets' credentials over what he called biased coverage, and the lawsuit the three filed on 21 September.
story.why: It is the first judicial check on an escalating fight between the White House and the press corps, and the fact that a judge Trump himself appointed issued it undercuts the administration's framing of the case as partisan.

story.headline: PAM wins most seats in Morocco vote
story.summary: Morocco's monarchy-aligned PAM took the most seats in the country's first parliamentary election since last year's Gen Z protests.
story.display_body: Morocco's monarchy-aligned Authenticity and Modernity Party (PAM) won the most seats in Wednesday's parliamentary election, taking 97 of the 395 seats according to provisional results announced Thursday 24 September by Interior Minister Abdelouafi Laftit. The result pushed the incumbent prime minister's liberal National Rally of Independents (RNI) into second place; the Istiqlal Party took 65 seats and the Islamist Justice and Development Party (PJD) surged to 54 from just 13 in 2021, while turnout fell. Because King Mohammed VI appoints the prime minister from the largest party, PAM is now in line to lead the next government — one candidate floated is PAM's Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri, who would be only the second woman to head a government in the Arab region. This was the first national vote since last year's deadly Gen Z-led protests over jobs and public services, and defence and foreign affairs remain under royal control.
story.why: A change of governing party signals voter frustration with the economic record that fuelled the protests, though the monarchy's grip on the key portfolios limits how much any new government can actually change.

story.headline: Baltics sanction Russian oligarchs
story.summary: Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania imposed national sanctions on Usmanov and Fridman after the EU delisted them.
story.display_body: Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania imposed their own national sanctions on Thursday 24 September against Russian billionaires Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman, days after the EU dropped the pair from its sanctions list. [single-source]. The three Baltic states moved to keep restrictions on the two men — both regarded as close to the Kremlin — in place nationally after the EU's 22 September rollover of its Russia sanctions removed them at the urging of France and Luxembourg, a carve-out Kyiv had called "shameful."
story.why: it shows front-line EU states willing to patch what they see as holes the bloc's own compromise opened, and underlines how the delisting fractured the united front the sanctions regime is meant to project. SRF, 24.09.2026

story.headline: SNB keeps policy rate at zero
story.summary: The Swiss National Bank left its policy rate unchanged at 0% as inflation edged up to 0.8%.
story.display_body: The Swiss National Bank left its policy rate unchanged at 0% on Thursday 24 September, judging current monetary policy appropriate as inflation ticked up to 0.8%. In its quarterly assessment, the SNB said inflation rose from 0.6% in May to 0.8% in August — with goods inflation turning positive for the first time since May 2024, driven mainly by higher oil-product prices — and that medium-term inflationary pressure has increased only slightly. Its conditional inflation forecast, which assumes the rate stays at 0% throughout, puts average annual inflation at 0.7% for 2026 and 0.8% for both 2027 and 2028, all comfortably within the SNB's price-stability range; it expects Swiss growth of 1.5–2% this year. The bank flagged the Middle East and energy prices as the main sources of uncertainty and said it remains ready to intervene in currency markets, noting the franc's recent depreciation.
story.why: Holding at zero keeps Swiss mortgage and savings rates roughly where they are, and the SNB's read — that the inflation uptick is mostly imported energy rather than a domestic overheating — signals it sees no near-term need to move in either direction.

story.headline: Council of States rejects naturalisation bid
story.summary: The Council of States rejected the 'democracy initiative' to allow naturalisation after five years, sending it to a popular vote without backing.
story.display_body: The Council of States rejected the "democracy initiative" on naturalisation on Thursday 24 September by 34 votes to 9, following the National Council and sending the popular initiative toward a national vote without parliamentary backing. The initiative — "For a modern nationality," filed by the Aktion Vierviertel campaign — would let foreign residents apply for citizenship after five years of legal residence regardless of settlement-permit status, against the current requirement of at least ten years; one study cited in the debate ranks Switzerland's naturalisation rules the strictest in Europe after Cyprus. The centre-right majority called the change disproportionate and defended the existing division of naturalisation powers between Confederation, cantons and communes; the chamber also rejected any counter-proposal, by 28 votes to 17. Justice Minister Beat Jans said talks with the cantons on harmonising practices — without lowering the conditions — are under way.
story.why: With both chambers now opposed, the measure heads to voters as a straight up-or-down initiative, reopening a recurring Swiss debate over how hard it should be for long-settled residents, and the second and third generations, to become citizens.
